h1: Arizona Reassessment After Storm or Damage Demand Letter
metaTitle: Arizona Storm Damage Reassessment Demand Letter Tool
metaDescription: Generate an Arizona property tax reassessment letter after storm or casualty damage. Cite A.R.S. § 42-15157 and request a prorated valuation.
statuteCitation: A.R.S. § 42-15157 (Destruction of property after rolls closed; proration of valuation and taxes)
deadline: Consult A.R.S. § 42-15157 and your county assessor; act promptly after the damage
penalty: Valuation prorated from the lien date to the date of destruction, with taxes computed on the prorated amounts
introParagraph: When a monsoon, microburst, wildfire, flood, or hailstorm destroys part of your Arizona property after the assessment rolls have closed, you should not keep paying taxes on a value that no longer reflects reality. Arizona law lets the person liable for the taxes seek a reduced, prorated valuation. The county assessor will not necessarily adjust your value automatically, so a clear written request is worth sending. This page explains how Arizona's destroyed-property statute works and how to escalate if the assessor does not act.
lawExplanation: A.R.S. § 42-15157 applies when property is destroyed after the assessor closes the rolls. The owner may file a notice of claim, or the assessor may issue a notice of proposed correction. When the assessor finds the property was destroyed, the assessor prorates the valuation from the lien date to the date of destruction and gives the owner notice, and the county treasurer computes the taxes by applying the tax rate to the original valuation prorated for the period the property stood intact plus the reassessed value prorated for the balance of the year. Where the destruction results from a verifiable accident such as fire, flood, or another act of God, the assessor may keep the property's classification from the date of destruction for up to five years, or until an objectively verifiable change in use occurs, whichever comes first. Separately, a notice of claim under A.R.S. § 42-16254 can be filed with the assessor to correct a valuation or classification error; the tax officer has sixty days to respond, and silence is treated as consent. For broader valuation disputes, A.R.S. § 42-16051 allows a petition to the assessor within sixty days after the notice of valuation is mailed. Document the damage with dated photographs, insurance claims, repair estimates, and contractor reports.
letterStrategy: Address the letter to the county assessor where the property sits, identify the parcel by Assessor Parcel Number (APN), and state that you are requesting a prorated valuation for destroyed property under A.R.S. § 42-15157. Specify the date of the damaging event, the nature of the damage, and attach photographs, an insurance adjuster's report, and repair bids. Request a specific remedy: a prorated valuation from the date of destruction, an amended notice, and a corrected tax bill or refund of any overpaid taxes. Set a reasonable response date and state that if no action is taken you will file a notice of claim under A.R.S. § 42-16254. Send the letter by certified mail, return receipt requested, and keep proof of mailing.
proceduralNotes: The administrative steps are free. If the assessor refuses, a notice of claim under A.R.S. § 42-16254 starts a sixty-day response period for the tax officer; the board of equalization petition and any court appeal have their own deadlines in that section, and a court appeal of a valuation is governed by A.R.S. § 42-16201. Confirm the current text of A.R.S. § 42-15157 before relying on it, because legislation amending the section has been proposed.

faq.q: What qualifies as 'destroyed' property under Arizona law?
faq.a: A.R.S. § 42-15157 applies to property destroyed after the assessor closes the rolls, and for destruction by a verifiable accident such as fire, flood, or another act of God it lets the assessor keep the property's classification from the destruction date for up to five years or until a verifiable change in use. Partial damage may not qualify for proration, but you can still pursue a valuation correction through a notice of claim or the regular appeal process.

faq.q: How quickly should I notify the Arizona county assessor after storm damage?
faq.a: As soon as the damage is documented. Do not wait for repairs or insurance settlements. The statute does not give a single filing date that we have confirmed, so check A.R.S. § 42-15157 and ask your assessor's office which form it requires. Send your letter by certified mail and keep the receipt.

faq.q: Will my taxes be adjusted if I already paid the full amount?
faq.a: Under A.R.S. § 42-15157 the treasurer computes taxes on the prorated valuations. Ask in your letter for a corrected bill, and a refund or credit if you have already paid, and provide a current mailing address.

faq.q: What if the assessor ignores or denies my letter?
faq.a: You can file a notice of claim under A.R.S. § 42-16254; the tax officer then has sixty days to respond, and no written response within sixty days is treated as consent. You can also use the petition and appeal process starting with A.R.S. § 42-16051. Each step has its own deadline, so act promptly and consider consulting a property tax attorney.

faq.q: Do I need an attorney to send a reassessment letter in Arizona?
faq.a: No. Property owners can send the letter and file a notice of claim themselves. If your case proceeds to the board of equalization or the tax court, or the value involved is substantial, an Arizona property tax attorney or licensed tax agent can help.
